title: Assembly tutorial: x86-64 registers, NASM syntax, syscalls and functions — cv.cm
description: Learn x86-64 assembly on Linux with NASM: registers, arithmetic, jumps and loops, memory addressing, system calls, the calling convention and AT&T syntax.
h1: Assembly language tutorial for beginners (x86-64, NASM)
answer: Assembly language is a human-readable form of a processor's machine instructions: each line usually becomes one instruction such as `mov rax, 1` or `add rax, rbx`. You work directly with registers, memory addresses and the stack, with no variables, types or loops beyond what you build from jumps. This tutorial uses x86-64 on Linux with the NASM assembler: write a `.asm` file, assemble it with `nasm -f elf64`, and link it with `ld`.

sections.h: What assembly is and who uses it
body: Every processor family has its own instruction set and therefore its own assembly language. x86-64 (also called AMD64) runs most desktop PCs and servers; ARM (AArch64) runs most phones, Apple silicon Macs and many servers. An assembler translates assembly into machine code, and a linker combines the result into an executable.

Few programs are written entirely in assembly today. It is used in operating system kernels and bootloaders, performance-critical routines (cryptography, codecs, math libraries), embedded firmware, compiler development, security research and reverse engineering. Most often, developers read assembly to understand what a compiler produced or to debug a crash.

sections.h: Install NASM and run Hello, world
body: On Debian or Ubuntu, install the tools with `sudo apt install nasm binutils` (`binutils` provides the linker `ld`). This program calls the Linux kernel directly through system calls, so it needs no C library.

body.code:
; hello.asm - x86-64 Linux, NASM syntax
section .data
    msg     db "Hello, world!", 10   ; 10 = newline
    msglen  equ $ - msg              ; length computed by the assembler

section .text
    global _start

_start:
    mov     rax, 1          ; system call number 1 = write
    mov     rdi, 1          ; file descriptor 1 = stdout
    mov     rsi, msg        ; address of the bytes
    mov     rdx, msglen     ; number of bytes
    syscall

    mov     rax, 60         ; system call number 60 = exit
    xor     rdi, rdi        ; exit code 0
    syscall

nasm -f elf64 hello.asm -o hello.o
ld hello.o -o hello
./hello
# Hello, world!

body: `section .data` holds initialized data, `section .text` holds code, and `_start` is the entry point that `ld` looks for. Comments start with `;`. Without the final `exit` system call, the processor would keep executing whatever bytes follow and the program would crash.
Registers are small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU. x86-64 has 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers. Each can also be used in smaller parts.

head: Register
Common role
Smaller parts
rows: First three function or system call arguments
Values that must survive function calls (callee-saved)
Stack pointer: address of the top of the stack
Instruction pointer (changed only by jumps, calls, returns)

body: Data in memory is declared with `db` (byte, 8 bits), `dw` (word, 16), `dd` (doubleword, 32) and `dq` (quadword, 64). Uninitialized buffers go in `section .bss` with `resb`, `resq` and so on. Writing to a 32-bit register such as `eax` also clears the upper 32 bits of `rax`, which is why `xor eax, eax` is a common way to set `rax` to zero.

Most instructions take a destination first and a source second: `add rax, rbx` means `rax = rax + rbx`. There are no `if` or `while` statements; you compare values with `cmp`, which sets flags, and then use a conditional jump.

head: Instruction
Meaning
rows: Jump if equal, not equal, less, greater... (signed)
Put a value on the stack, take it off
Call a function, return from it

body.code:
; sum.asm - add 1..10, return the result as the exit code
section .text
    global _start

_start:
    xor     rax, rax        ; sum = 0
    mov     rcx, 1          ; i = 1
.loop:
    cmp     rcx, 10
    jg      .done           ; if i > 10, leave the loop
    add     rax, rcx        ; sum += i
    inc     rcx             ; i++
    jmp     .loop
.done:
    mov     rdi, rax        ; exit code = sum
    mov     rax, 60         ; exit
    syscall

nasm -f elf64 sum.asm -o sum.o && ld sum.o -o sum
./sum; echo $?
# 55

body: Labels starting with a dot, like `.loop`, are local to the previous normal label. `jl` and `jg` treat values as signed; `jb` and `ja` are the unsigned versions.

Square brackets mean "the memory at this address". An address can combine a base register, an index register multiplied by 1, 2, 4 or 8, and a constant: `[base + index*scale + offset]`. This makes array access a single instruction.

body.code:
section .data
    nums    dq 3, 1, 4, 1, 5         ; five 64-bit integers
    count   equ ($ - nums) / 8

section .text
    global _start

_start:
    xor     rax, rax                 ; total = 0
    xor     rcx, rcx                 ; index = 0
.next:
    add     rax, [nums + rcx*8]      ; total += nums[index]
    inc     rcx
    cmp     rcx, count
    jl      .next
    mov     rdi, rax                 ; exit code 14
    mov     rax, 60
    syscall

body: `mov rax, nums` loads the address, while `mov rax, [nums]` loads the value stored there. `lea rsi, [rbx + 8]` computes an address without reading memory. When the size is not clear from a register, state it: `mov qword [rbx], 0`.

On Linux, functions follow the System V AMD64 ABI. Integer arguments go in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `rcx`, `r8`, `r9`; the return value is in `rax`. A function must preserve `rbx`, `rbp`, `r12`–`r15` and `rsp`, and `rsp` must be a multiple of 16 just before a `call`. Following these rules lets assembly call C functions such as `printf`, and lets C call assembly.

body.code:
; square.asm - define a function and call printf from the C library
    extern  printf
    global  main

section .data
    fmt     db "%ld squared is %ld", 10, 0

section .text
square:                         ; long square(long x)
    mov     rax, rdi
    imul    rax, rdi
    ret

main:
    push    rbx                 ; save rbx; also aligns rsp to 16
    mov     rbx, 7
    mov     rdi, rbx
    call    square              ; rax = 49
    lea     rdi, [rel fmt]      ; argument 1: format string
    mov     rsi, rbx            ; argument 2
    mov     rdx, rax            ; argument 3
    xor     eax, eax            ; varargs: no vector registers used
    call    printf wrt ..plt
    xor     eax, eax            ; return 0 from main
    pop     rbx
    ret

section .note.GNU-stack noalloc noexec nowrite progbits

nasm -f elf64 square.asm -o square.o
gcc square.o -o square
./square
# 7 squared is 49

body: Linking with `gcc` adds the C runtime, which calls `main`. `[rel fmt]` and `wrt ..plt` produce position-independent code, which modern Linux distributions use by default. The last line marks the stack as non-executable and avoids a linker warning.

Assembly has no exceptions. A Linux system call that fails returns a negative error number in `rax` (for example -2, `ENOENT`, "no such file"), so you test the sign after each call. C library functions report errors through their return value and `errno`. Hardware faults, such as reading an invalid address or dividing by zero, stop the program with a signal (segmentation fault or floating point exception).

body.code:
mov     rax, 2              ; system call 2 = open
    lea     rdi, [rel path]     ; path is a zero-terminated string
    xor     esi, esi            ; flags: O_RDONLY
    syscall
    test    rax, rax
    js      .open_failed        ; negative result = -errno
    mov     r12, rax            ; success: rax is the file descriptor

sections.h: A small complete program: print a number in decimal
body: Printing a number means converting it to digits yourself. This program computes 1 + 2 + ... + 100, divides repeatedly by 10 to get the digits from right to left, and writes them with one system call.

body.code:
section .bss
    buf     resb 32

section .text
    global _start

_start:
    xor     rax, rax
    mov     rcx, 100
.sum:
    add     rax, rcx
    loop    .sum                ; rcx -= 1, repeat while rcx != 0
    lea     rsi, [buf + 31]
    mov     byte [rsi], 10      ; newline at the end of the buffer
    mov     rbx, 10
.digit:
    xor     rdx, rdx            ; div uses rdx:rax as the dividend
    div     rbx                 ; rax = quotient, rdx = remainder
    add     dl, '0'             ; remainder to ASCII digit
    dec     rsi
    mov     [rsi], dl
    test    rax, rax
    jnz     .digit
    mov     rdx, buf + 32
    sub     rdx, rsi            ; length = end - start
    mov     rax, 1              ; write(1, rsi, rdx)
    mov     rdi, 1
    syscall
    mov     rax, 60             ; exit(0)
    xor     rdi, rdi
    syscall
; prints 5050

body.note: Common beginner mistakes: forgetting the `exit` system call; using `div` without clearing `rdx` first (the result overflows and the program crashes); expecting `rcx` and `r11` to survive a `syscall` (the kernel overwrites them); calling C functions with a misaligned stack; confusing an address with the value at that address (`msg` vs `[msg]`); and mixing up Intel and AT&T operand order when reading examples.

sections.h: AT&T vs Intel syntax, and ARM
body: The same x86-64 instruction can be written in two syntaxes. NASM and most Intel and Microsoft documentation use Intel syntax. The GNU assembler (`as`), GCC output and `objdump` use AT&T syntax by default; `objdump -d -M intel` and `gcc -S -masm=intel` switch to Intel syntax.

ARM processors use a different instruction set. AArch64 has 31 general-purpose 64-bit registers (`x0`–`x30`), fixed 32-bit instruction encodings, and a load/store design: arithmetic works only on registers, and memory is accessed with `ldr` and `str`. On Linux, the system call number goes in `x8` and the call is made with `svc #0`.

body.code:
// AArch64 Linux, GNU as syntax: exit(0)
    mov     x0, #0          // exit status
    mov     x8, #93         // system call 93 = exit
    svc     #0

ul: The NASM manual for directives, macros and output formats.
Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manuals for the exact behavior of every instruction.
The System V AMD64 ABI document for calling conventions and stack layout.
Compile small C functions with `gcc -O2 -S -masm=intel` (or an online compiler explorer) and read the generated assembly.

faq.q: Is assembly language still worth learning?
faq.a: Yes, for understanding how computers work, debugging crashes, reading compiler output, security work and embedded development. Writing whole applications in assembly is rarely practical today.

faq.q: Is x86 assembly the same as ARM assembly?
faq.a: No. They are different instruction sets with different registers, instructions and encodings. The concepts (registers, memory, jumps, calling conventions) transfer, but the code does not.

faq.q: What is the difference between NASM and GAS?
faq.a: NASM is a standalone assembler that uses Intel syntax. GAS, the GNU assembler, is used by GCC and defaults to AT&T syntax, although it also accepts Intel syntax with `.intel_syntax noprefix`.

faq.q: Does this code run on Windows or macOS?
faq.a: Not unchanged. The instructions are the same on any x86-64 system, but system call numbers, the executable format and the calling convention differ. Windows uses a different calling convention, and Apple silicon Macs use ARM instead of x86-64.
